summary: Give the Free cash flow to equity (FCFE) calculator the cash flow from operation, the FCFF, the ending total debt and the depreciation and amortization and it returns corporate tax rate. Think of it as a shortcut for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Free cash flow to equity (FCFE) calculator work?
sections.html:
The Free cash flow to equity (FCFE) calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports corporate tax rate in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the calculate using); then you type in the cash flow from operation (CFO), the FCFF, the ending total debt and the depreciation and amortization.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Free cash flow to equity (FCFE) calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Corporate tax rate=(free cash flow to equity (FCFE) − FCFF + interest expense − net borrowing) ÷ interest expense
Fixed capital investment=depreciation and amortization − free cash flow to equity (FCFE) + net borrowing + net income − working capital investment
Fixed capital investment=depreciation and amortization × corporate tax rate − EBITDA × corporate tax rate + EBITDA − free cash flow to equity (FCFE) + interest expense × corporate tax rate − interest expense + net borrowing − working capital investment
Fixed capital investment=depreciation and amortization − EBIT × corporate tax rate + EBIT − free cash flow to equity (FCFE) + interest expense × corporate tax rate − interest expense + net borrowing − working capital investment
Fixed capital investment=cash flow from operation (CFO) − free cash flow to equity (FCFE) + net borrowing
Corporate tax rate=(depreciation and amortization − EBITDA + interest expense + net income) ÷ (depreciation and amortization − EBITDA + interest expense)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Free cash flow to equity (FCFE) calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the cash flow from operation, the FCFF and the ending total debt — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Free cash flow to equity (FCFE) calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns corporate tax rate, derived from the cash flow from operation, the FCFF and the ending total debt. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Free cash flow to equity (FCFE) calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the cash flow from operation, the FCFF, the ending total debt and the depreciation and amortization, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter net income in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Net income opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Free cash flow to equity (FCFE) calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
